derivations.claim: Let $p,q\in\mathbb Z$ satisfy $\gcd(p,q)=1$. Bézout's identity gives $r,s\in\mathbb Z$ with $ps-qr=1$. The matrix with columns $(p,q)$ and $(r,s)$ lies in $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)$, so it induces a homeomorphism of $\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$. The image of the first coordinate circle is embedded, essential, and represents $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$. Reversing its parameter negates both coefficients, so the unoriented curve is unchanged.

If $\gamma$ is an essential simple closed curve on $T$, it is nonseparating; cutting along it gives an annulus. An arc joining the two annulus boundary circles closes to a simple curve $\delta$ meeting $\gamma$ once, so the algebraic intersection is $[\gamma]\cdot[\delta]=\pm1$. Writing $[\gamma]=p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ and $[\delta]=a[\mu]+b[\lambda]$ gives $pb-qa=\pm1$ because the ordered basis has intersection form $\pm1$. Any common divisor of $p,q$ would divide $pb-qa$, so $\gcd(p,q)=1$.

Suppose $\gamma_0,\gamma_1$ are essential simple closed curves whose primitive classes agree up to sign. Reverse one orientation if necessary so their classes agree, and isotope them to be transverse. Let $v$ be their common primitive class and let $A=\mathbb R^2/\langle T_v\rangle$ be the cyclic cover of $T$ corresponding to the subgroup generated by $v$. A lift of each curve to $A$ is an embedded essential circle representing the generator of $H_1(A;\mathbb Z)$. Their algebraic intersection in the annulus $A$ is zero, so if they meet the signed crossing count in a fundamental period has both signs. Lift these circles to the universal cover $\mathbb R^2$ of $A$. Their chosen lifts are proper lines invariant under the same translation $T_v$; they have the same two ends at infinity. Opposite-sign crossings on this pair of lines have a bounded complementary disk between subarcs, by the Jordan curve theorem. Among all such disks choose one with the fewest interior intersections with lifted curves, and among ties one of least transverse width modulo the deck translations. Any lifted arc entering its interior cuts off a disk with fewer interior intersections; any nontrivial translate meeting it yields a disk of smaller transverse width. Thus its interior misses every lift and translate, so it projects injectively to an embedded bigon in $T$. Isotoping one curve across this bigon removes exactly two intersections and creates none. Since the original intersection set is finite, repetition terminates and makes the curves disjoint. Cutting $T$ along $\gamma_0$ gives an annulus, and the disjoint essential curve $\gamma_1$ is parallel to its core, so the two curves cobound a subannulus. Isotopy across that annulus carries $\gamma_0$ to $\gamma_1$. Thus the primitive class modulo simultaneous sign determines exactly one unoriented isotopy class.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, assuming the Axiom of Countable Choice,
an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid $\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

derivations.claim: In $S^3=\{(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2=1\}$, the standard Hopf link is $H=\{z_1z_2=0\}$. On its complement, $f(z_1,z_2)=z_1z_2/|z_1z_2|$ is a submersion to $S^1$. Writing $r=|z_1|^2$, $\theta=\arg z_1$, and $\phi=\arg z_2$, a fiber is $0<r<1$, $\phi=-\theta+\text{constant}$, hence an annulus. For base angle $s\in[0,2\pi]$, transport by $\theta_s=\theta+\chi(r)s$, $\phi_s=\phi+(1-\chi(r))s$, where $\chi=1$ near $r=0$ and $\chi=0$ near $r=1$, fixes both boundary circles at $s=2\pi$ and makes one full annular twist between them. The sign is determined by the signed linking of the positive normal push-off of the core with the core: changing the handedness of the Hopf band reverses the twist. With $a\cdot_F b=+1$, the positive twist about $a$ acts by $b\mapsto a+b$, while the negative twist about $b$ acts by $a\mapsto a+b$. Hence the two band monodromies have the stated actions $R_a$ and $L_b$.

The square plumbing is the Murasugi sum in Construction 5.37 of [F3]. Theorem 5.38 of [F3] gives a fibration with fiber $F$ and return map the composition of the two Hopf-band monodromies extended by the identity; in the stipulated order, step 1.1 identifies it as $R_a\circ L_b$. Example 5.39 of [F3] identifies the boundary of the opposite-handed sum as the standard figure-eight knot. Deleting the binding neighborhood as in [F1] therefore gives the stated exterior as the mapping torus.

Each annulus has Euler characteristic $0$, and the plumbing square has Euler characteristic $1$, so $\chi(F)=0+0-1=-1$. The plumbing is connected, oriented, and has one boundary component by the stated gluing; hence $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$ gives $g(F)=1$. Thus $F$ is a once-punctured torus.

In the ordered basis $([a],[b])$, the columns of $R_a$ are $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$, while the columns of $L_b$ are $(1,1)$ and $(0,1)$. Their product is $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Inclusion of the once-punctured torus into the torus obtained by capping its sole boundary induces an isomorphism on $H_1$, since attaching a disk along the boundary adds no 1-cycle or 2-cycle relation in degree one. Extending the boundary-fixing monodromy by the identity on that disk therefore has the same displayed action.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$ uses the product Euclidean norm induced by the chosen trivialization. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

A compact orientable three-manifold $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. A properly embedded surface is **incompressible** if it admits no embedded disk whose interior misses the surface and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in it. A boundary subsurface is **$\pi_1$-injective** if the inclusion of each component induces an injection on fundamental groups. A **pared pair** is a pair $(M,P)$ in which $M$ is compact, orientable and irreducible, and $P$ is a possibly empty compact subsurface of $\partial M$ whose pairwise disjoint components are $\pi_1$-injective annuli or tori, every noncyclic abelian subgroup of $\pi_1(M)$ is conjugate into $\pi_1$ of a component of $P$ up to base-path conjugacy, and every map of pairs
$$
(S^1\times I,S^1\times\partial I)\longrightarrow(M,P)
$$
that induces injections on fundamental groups is homotopic through maps of pairs into $P$, so its boundary remains in $P$ during the homotopy. Write $\partial_0M=\partial M\setminus\operatorname{int}P$. A **horoball** is a region bounded by a horosphere, a Euclidean plane or sphere tangent to the ideal boundary at one point. The **peripheral subgroup** for a component of $P$ is the image of its fundamental group in $\pi_1(M)$, recorded up to conjugacy. A **hyperbolic structure** on $(M,P)$ is a curvature $-1$ metric on $\operatorname{int}M$ described by an atlas of charts into $\mathbb H^3$ whose transition maps are in $\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$. Its developing map $\operatorname{dev}$ from the universal cover and holonomy homomorphism $\rho:\pi_1(M)\to\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$ satisfy $\operatorname{dev}(gx)=\rho(g)\operatorname{dev}(x)$. The metric is **complete** when it is geodesically complete. A **cusp** corresponding to a component of $P$ is a quotient of a horoball by the associated peripheral subgroup. The hyperbolic volume is the integral of the Riemannian volume density over $\operatorname{int}M$; the structure has **finite volume** when this integral is finite.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let
$(M,g)$ be a connected, boundaryless, finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold
that is complete and whose sectional curvature satisfies $K\le0$ at every
tangent two-plane. Then for every $p\in M$:

1. the exponential map $\exp_p:T_pM\to M$ is a smooth covering map when its
   domain carries the pulled-back metric $\tilde g:=\exp_p^*g$;
2. $(T_pM,\tilde g)$ is complete and $T_pM$ is simply connected, so $\exp_p$ is
   a **universal cover** of $M$;
3. if in addition $M$ is simply connected, then $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism
   for every $p$, and $M$ is diffeomorphic to the Euclidean space $T_pM$.

The curvature sign is the one of [[def-sectional-curvature]], so $K\le0$
includes the flat case; no lower bound on curvature, no compactness and no
dimension restriction (other than finiteness) are assumed. The completeness of
$(T_pM,\tilde g)$ is a conclusion, not a hypothesis: without it the pulled-back
metric need not be complete even for a local diffeomorphism of a complete
manifold.

Assume exactly $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the declared constant-curvature
interface. Let $(M,g)$ be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary
of constant sectional curvature $K\in\mathbb R$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a
nondegenerate interval containing $0$, and let
$\gamma:I\to M$ be a unit-speed affinely parametrized geodesic. Put
$T=\dot\gamma$ and define
$$
s_K(t)=\begin{cases}\sin(\sqrt K\,t)/\sqrt K,&K>0,\\ t,&K=0,\\ \sinh(\sqrt{-K}\,t)/\sqrt{-K},&K<0.\end{cases}
$$
Then the normal Jacobi fields $J$ with $J(0)=0$ are exactly
$$J(t)=s_K(t)E(t),$$
where $E$ is a unique parallel normal field along $\gamma$. The tangential
Jacobi fields are exactly
$$J(t)=(at+b)\dot\gamma(t),\qquad a,b\in\mathbb R.$$
No completeness is assumed. If an endpoint of $I$ is included, derivatives there
are one-sided.

A **universal covering space** of $B$ is a covering map $p:\widetilde B\to B$ whose total space $\widetilde B$ is simply connected ([[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]], [[def-simply-connected]]).

For a covering $p:E\to B$, a **deck transformation** is an isomorphism $h:E\to E$ over $B$, so $p\circ h=p$ ([[def-map-and-isomorphism-of-covering-spaces]]). Deck transformations form the **deck group** $\operatorname{Deck}(p)$ under composition, and this group acts on $E$ by evaluation ([[def-group]], [[def-group-action]]).

For a path-connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected base $B$, the deck group of a universal cover is isomorphic to $\pi_1(B,b_0)$. With the library's traversal-order path product the monodromy action is a right action, and the assignment carrying a loop class to the deck transformation that moves the chosen point of the fibre to the corresponding lifted endpoint is itself an isomorphism; no path reversal is inserted.

An **isometry** $F:(M,g)\to(N,h)$ is a diffeomorphism with $F^*h=g$. A **local isometry** is a smooth local diffeomorphism with $F^*h=g$. An **isometric immersion** is a smooth immersion satisfying that same pullback identity.

Use [[def-pullback-riemannian-metric]] and [[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]. Positivity forces injective differential by [[prop-pullback-of-a-riemannian-metric-is-riemannian-exactly-for-immersions]]. In equal dimensions on boundaryless manifolds, the inverse function theorem as applied in the next proposition makes a metric-preserving smooth map a local isometry. At a boundary the definition retains the local-diffeomorphism requirement. An isometric immersion need not have equal source and target dimensions.

Let $F:(M,g)\to(N,h)$ be a local Riemannian isometry between smooth Riemannian manifolds without boundary. For every $p\in M$, there are open neighborhoods $U\ni p$ and $V\ni F(p)$ such that $f=F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism and
$$df\bigl(\nabla^M_XY\bigr)=\nabla^N_{f_*X}(f_*Y)\circ f$$
for all smooth vector fields $X,Y$ on $U$, where $\nabla^M$ and $\nabla^N$ are the Levi-Civita connections.

Consequently, if $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval with nonempty interior, $\gamma:I\to M$ is smooth, and $W$ is a smooth vector field along $\gamma$, then
$$D_t^N\bigl(dF_{\gamma(t)}W(t)\bigr)=dF_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(D_t^M W(t)\bigr).$$
In particular, $F\circ\gamma$ is an affinely parametrized geodesic whenever $\gamma$ is. No completeness, connectedness, surjectivity, or length-minimizing hypothesis is required.

Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering, let $\alpha:I\to B$ be a path, and let $e_0\in E$ satisfy $p(e_0)=\alpha(0)$. There is a unique path $\widetilde\alpha:I\to E$ with $\widetilde\alpha(0)=e_0$ and $p\circ\widetilde\alpha=\alpha$.

By [F2], the complete simply connected universal cover $\widetilde M$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^3$. Along each radial unit-speed geodesic from a fixed point, [F3] says the differential of the exponential map multiplies angular vectors by $\sinh r$, while its radial differential preserves length. Thus in polar coordinates the pulled-back metric is $dr^2+\sinh^2(r)g_{S^2}$, the standard hyperbolic metric; the exponential map identifies $\widetilde M$ isometrically with $\mathbb H^3$. By [F4], $\Gamma=\pi_1(M)$ acts freely and properly discontinuously by deck isometries; compactness of $M$ makes the action cocompact.

Every nonidentity element of $\Gamma$ is loxodromic. A Möbius map $z\mapsto(az+b)/(cz+d)$ has fixed-point equation $cz^2+(d-a)z-b=0$ on the boundary sphere. If there are two distinct fixed points, conjugate them to $0,\infty$; the map then has form $z\mapsto \lambda z$. If $|\lambda|=1$ and $\lambda
e1$, its extension fixes the axis joining $0$ to $\infty$, contrary to the free deck action [F4]. If $|\lambda|
e1$, it preserves that axis and translates it nontrivially. If the fixed-point equation has a double root, conjugate it to $\infty$; the map has form $z\mapsto az+b$, and its only fixed point is $\infty$ precisely when $a=1$ and $b
e0$. This is parabolic: the upper-half-space distance formula gives $\cosh d((0,t),(b,t))=1+|b|^2/(2t^2)$, so its displacement tends to zero as $t	o\infty$. To exclude such a parabolic in a cocompact deck group, choose compact $K$ with $\Gamma K=\mathbb H^3$ and points $y_n$ whose displacement tends to zero. Choose $h_n\in\Gamma$ so $x_n=h_ny_n\in K$ and put $\gamma_n=h_n\gamma h_n^{-1}$. The points $x_n$ and $\gamma_nx_n$ lie in a fixed compact neighborhood of $K$, so proper discontinuity permits only finitely many $\gamma_n$. Along a subsequence this element is constant and $x_n$ converges in $K$; the displacement limit makes it fix the limit point, contradicting freeness. Hence every nonidentity element has two fixed endpoints and preserves a unique axis with nonzero translation.

Fix $\gamma\ne1$ and let $C_\Gamma(\gamma)=\{\delta\in\Gamma:\delta\gamma=\gamma\delta\}$. Commutation preserves the attracting and repelling endpoints of $\gamma$ individually, hence preserves its axis and acts there by a signed translation. The signed translation map $\tau:C_\Gamma(\gamma)\to\mathbb R$ is a homomorphism. It is injective: an element in its kernel fixes every point on the axis, and [F4] makes it the identity. Its image is discrete: if infinitely many elements had bounded signed translations, their images of a fixed point on the axis would lie in a compact segment, contradicting proper discontinuity in [F4]. Every discrete subgroup of $(\mathbb R,+)$ is cyclic, so $C_\Gamma(\gamma)$ is cyclic.

If $H\le\Gamma$ were isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$, choose $\gamma\in H\setminus\{1\}$. Since $H$ is abelian, $H\subseteq C_\Gamma(\gamma)$, contradicting step 4.1 because a cyclic group has no subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$. Therefore no such $H$ exists.

The two assumed basis multipliers are $1$, so this linear part is the identity for every loop in $\pi_1(T_v)$.

Fix a Euclidean metric in one link chart and transport it through the similarity charts. The metric is independent of the transport path, because every loop has identity linear holonomy and translations preserve the Euclidean metric. This gives a global flat metric $g_v$ on the compact torus $T_v$, hence a complete one. Its lift to the universal cover is complete as well: any geodesic projects to a geodesic on the complete torus, extends there, and the extension lifts through the covering. The lifted Euclidean charts develop to a local isometry into $\mathbb R^2$. Every finite straight segment starting at a point in the image lifts to its endpoint: a partial lift has finite length, is therefore Cauchy, and extends from its limit by the local isometry. Hence the development is onto. For a small Euclidean ball about any point, lifting its radial segments from each preimage gives disjoint isometric copies of that ball; lifting the reverse radial segments shows these copies exhaust its preimage. Thus the development is a covering, and since $\mathbb R^2$ is simply connected it is an isometry. Deck transformations have identity linear part by the trivial link holonomy, so act by translations. Compactness of $T_v$ makes their translation vectors a rank-two lattice $\Lambda_v$. The assembled end is therefore the quotient of a horoball by $\Lambda_v$, with metric $dr^2+e^{-2r}g_v$ in horospherical depth $r$. A path escaping toward the ideal vertex has length at least the change in $r$, so the end is complete. Repeating this argument at each of the finitely many vertices proves completeness at every end. Each removed vertex tail is contained in a rank-two horocusp and has finite volume by [F4]. There are finitely many tetrahedra and vertices, so the glued manifold has finite total volume.

The part left after truncating all cusp ends is compact. Let $(x_n)$ be Cauchy. If infinitely many terms lie in this compact part, a subsequence converges there, and the Cauchy property forces the whole sequence to the same limit. Otherwise $(x_n)$ is eventually in the union of the finitely many cusp ends. Distinct cusp boundary tori are disjoint compact subsets of the compact core, so their pairwise distances have a positive minimum; every path between different ends crosses the corresponding boundary tori. Hence a Cauchy tail cannot switch ends and eventually lies in one cusp $T^2\times[0,\infty)$. Fix a term $x_N$ in this tail. Any path from $x_N$ to a point at cusp depth $t$ has length at least $|t-t(x_N)|$ if it stays in the cusp and at least $t+t(x_N)$ if it exits through the boundary. Since the tail stays within bounded distance of $x_N$, its depths are bounded. It is therefore contained in a compact truncation $T^2\times[0,R]$, where a Cauchy sequence converges. Thus the full metric is complete. Together with step 3.2 and the curvature $-1$ charts from step 1.1, this is a complete finite-volume hyperbolic structure as defined in [F5].

Let $\overline M$ be a compact connected oriented three-manifold whose boundary is a disjoint union of tori $T_1,\ldots,T_k$. Choose an ordered integral basis $([\mu_i],[\lambda_i])$ for each $H_1(T_i;\mathbb Z)$. A **slope** on $T_i$ is an unoriented isotopy class of essential simple closed curves whose homology class is $p_i[\mu_i]+q_i[\lambda_i]$ for a primitive pair $(p_i,q_i)\in\mathbb Z^2$; simultaneous negation gives the same unoriented slope. The primitive-pair correspondence gives exactly one such slope for each primitive pair modulo sign. The **ordinary Dehn filling** along a tuple of slopes indexed by $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ attaches an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to each $T_i$, $i\in J$, by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{*\}]$ to the chosen slope. The gluing maps are part of the filling data; $i\notin J$ means that the cusp is left unfilled, denoted by the parameter $\infty$.

For a hyperbolic deformation, the **generalized cone-filling parameter space** at each cusp is the one-point compactification $\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$ of the real coefficient plane, with $\infty$ denoting the complete cusp. A primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ is an ordinary smooth filling coefficient. If a realized generalized parameter lies on the ray $g_i=r_i(p_i,q_i)$ with $r_i>0$ and $(p_i,q_i)$ primitive integral, its topological core direction is the ordinary slope $(p_i,q_i)$ and its cone angle is $2\pi/r_i$. Only $r_i=1$ is the ordinary smooth filling; $r_i>1$ describes a cone or orbifold completion and does not turn the nonprimitive vector $g_i$ into a slope.

A compact orientable three-manifold $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. A properly embedded surface is **incompressible** if it admits no embedded disk whose interior misses the surface and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in it. A boundary subsurface is **$\pi_1$-injective** if the inclusion of each component induces an injection on fundamental groups. A **pared pair** is a pair $(M,P)$ in which $M$ is compact, orientable and irreducible, and $P$ is a possibly empty compact subsurface of $\partial M$ whose pairwise disjoint components are $\pi_1$-injective annuli or tori, every noncyclic abelian subgroup of $\pi_1(M)$ is conjugate into $\pi_1$ of a component of $P$ up to base-path conjugacy, and every map of pairs
$$
(S^1\times I,S^1\times\partial I)\longrightarrow(M,P)
$$
that induces injections on fundamental groups is homotopic through maps of pairs into $P$, so its boundary remains in $P$ during the homotopy. Write $\partial_0M=\partial M\setminus\operatorname{int}P$. A **horoball** is a region bounded by a horosphere, a Euclidean plane or sphere tangent to the ideal boundary at one point. The **peripheral subgroup** for a component of $P$ is the image of its fundamental group in $\pi_1(M)$, recorded up to conjugacy. A **hyperbolic structure** on $(M,P)$ is a curvature $-1$ metric on $\operatorname{int}M$ described by an atlas of charts into $\mathbb H^3$ whose transition maps are in $\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$. Its developing map $\operatorname{dev}$ from the universal cover and holonomy homomorphism $\rho:\pi_1(M)\to\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$ satisfy $\operatorname{dev}(gx)=\rho(g)\operatorname{dev}(x)$. The metric is **complete** when it is geodesically complete. A **cusp** corresponding to a component of $P$ is a quotient of a horoball by the associated peripheral subgroup. The hyperbolic volume is the integral of the Riemannian volume density over $\operatorname{int}M$; the structure has **finite volume** when this integral is finite.

Suppose that around every finite edge the product of its incident complex shape parameters is $1$ and the sum of its dihedral angles is $2\pi$. For each ideal vertex $v$, choose a basis $(\alpha_v,\beta_v)$ of the fundamental group of its torus link and suppose the cusp multipliers satisfy $H(\alpha_v)=H(\beta_v)=1$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume AC. Every nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ is isometric to $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ for a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The covering is a universal Riemannian covering and identifies $\Gamma$ with the fundamental group up to the usual basepoint conjugacies. Its completeness and quotient presentation are conclusions from the stated metric hypotheses. The orientation-preserving isometry group of the model is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with its usual Möbius boundary action.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant curvature $-1$ and finite volume. Then $M$ is a compact core together with finitely many pairwise disjoint standard torus cusp ends. Each end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ of a horoball by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of these open ends is compact. The number of cusps may be zero. In particular, the standard cusp decomposition in the general rigidity construction follows from the complete finite-volume metric, with no knot or triangulation assumption.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be a connected oriented complete finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold, with a compact smooth core $N$ and $k\ge1$ standard rank-two torus cusp ends. Thus $M$ is the interior of $N$ and each end has metric $dt^2+e^{-2t}g_i$, where $g_i$ is a flat torus metric. Let $\rho_0:\pi_1(N)\to G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be its holonomy. Choose a positively oriented basis $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$ for each oriented horotorus, so its translation lattice can be normalized to $\langle1,\tau_i^0\rangle$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0>0$.

The germ of representations modulo conjugacy at $[\rho_0]$ is a smooth complex manifold of dimension $k$. The functions $s_i(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}^2\rho(\mu_i)$ are local holomorphic coordinates near their values $s_i=4$. Trace squared is well defined in $G$, independently of an $SL_2$ lift.

Augment a nearby representation by choosing one common invariant line for each peripheral subgroup, and quotient these data by simultaneous conjugacy. The germ of this augmented space at the complete representation and its unique peripheral fixed lines is a smooth complex $k$-manifold. It has holomorphic coordinates $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$, where $u_i$ is the eigenvalue-ratio logarithm for $\mu_i$ on the selected line, and the forgetful map is
$$s_i=4\cosh^2(u_i/2).$$
The corresponding logarithms $v_i$ for $\lambda_i$ are holomorphic and satisfy
$$v_i(u)=\tau_i(u)u_i,\qquad \tau_i(0)=\tau_i^0,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)>0$$
on a sufficiently small neighborhood. In particular $u_i=0$ if and only if $v_i=0$, and for $k=1$ one has $v(u)=\tau^0u+O(u^2)$. No positive or nondegenerate ideal triangulation is assumed. The statement concerns the augmented space, not a single-valued eigenvalue logarithm on the ordinary conjugacy quotient.

Assume AC. Let $k\ge1$ and let $\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_k$ be holomorphic on a neighborhood of $0\in\mathbb C^k$, with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(0)\ne0$. Put $v_i(u)=u_i\tau_i(u)$. At a coordinate with $u_i\ne0$, define real coefficients $(p_i,q_i)$ by
$$p_i u_i+q_i v_i(u)=2\pi i;$$
at $u_i=0$ define its parameter to be $\infty$ in the one-point compactification $S_i=\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$.

There are neighborhoods $U$ of $0$ and $V$ of $(\infty,\ldots,\infty)$ in $\prod_iS_i$ for which this parameter map is a homeomorphism $U\to V$. One may take $V=\prod_i(\{(p,q):p^2+q^2>R^2\}\cup\{\infty\})$ for a sufficiently large $R$. Every such tuple has a unique small simultaneous solution, with $u_i=0$ exactly at the unfilled coordinates. Uniformly as the tuple tends to the complete point, writing $w_i=2\pi i/(p_i+q_i\tau_i(0))$ for finite coordinates and $w_i=0$ at $\infty$, one has
$$u_i=w_i+O(|w_i|\|w\|_\infty),\qquad \|u\|_\infty\le\tfrac43\|w\|_\infty.$$
This analytic assertion allows real coefficients of either orientation. Primitive integral coefficients are included, but no geometric completion is asserted by the equations alone.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be a connected oriented complete finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold with a compact smooth core and $k\ge1$ disjoint standard torus cusp ends. Choose positively oriented peripheral bases $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$. Let $\rho_u$, for $u$ near $0$ in $\mathbb C^k$, be the augmented holonomy family supplied by the augmented holonomy-coordinate theorem, based at the complete holonomy $\rho_0$. Thus the logarithms satisfy $v_i(u)=\tau_i(u)u_i$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)>0$.

After shrinking this neighborhood, there are smooth hyperbolic metrics $g_u$ on $M$, possibly incomplete, with holonomy $\rho_u$. They depend smoothly on the real and imaginary parts of $u$ on every compact subset, and $g_0$ is the given complete metric. Each end with $u_i=0$ is a complete finite-volume translation cusp. Each end with $u_i\ne0$ has an explicit developing map onto the punctured tube about its peripheral axis, with the angular and axial periods specified by $u_i,v_i$.

Suppose $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ and, for every $i\in J$, a primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ satisfies
$$p_i u_i+q_i v_i(u)=2\pi i,$$
while $u_i=0$ for $i\notin J$. Then $g_u$ extends across all ends in $J$ to a smooth complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric on the ordinary Dehn filling whose meridians are $p_i\mu_i+q_i\lambda_i$. For arbitrary supplied orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphisms realizing these same slopes, the resulting topological filling is orientation-preservingly and core-preservingly homeomorphic to this realization, by a homeomorphism equal to the identity on the truncated original manifold. Transporting the realization's smooth structure and metric through this homeomorphism gives the asserted smooth hyperbolic metric on that supplied filling. No assertion is made about a separately prescribed smooth structure for an arbitrary topological gluing. The added cores are ordinary smooth geodesics, with no cone or orbifold singularity. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Define the standard figure-eight knot $K_8$ to be the oriented closure of the three-strand geometric braid $(\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2$. Its endpoint permutation is a $3$-cycle, so this closure has one component.

Let $\Delta_0=[0,1,2,3]$ and $\Delta_1=[0',1',2',3']$ be oriented ideal tetrahedra with orientation-reversing affine face maps
$$[0,1,2]\to[3',1',2'],\quad [0,1,3]\to[0',1',2'],\quad [0,2,3]\to[0',1',3'],\quad [1,2,3]\to[0',2',3'].$$
This is the two-tetrahedron ideal triangulation obtained from the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram by cutting along crossing arcs, identifying upper and lower polyhedron faces with equal region labels, and collapsing the two bigon faces. Its edge classes are
$$\{01,02,23,0'1',1'3',2'3'\},\qquad \{12,03,13,1'2',0'2',0'3'\};$$
each has valence six, and the unique ideal vertex link is a torus. Put shape $z_1$ on $01,23$, shape $z_2$ on $03,12$, and shape $z_3$ on $02,13$ in $\Delta_0$; put shape $w_1$ on $0'1',2'3'$, shape $w_2$ on $0'3',1'2'$, and shape $w_3$ on $0'2',1'3'$ in $\Delta_1$. Unfold the eight cusp-link triangles by the face maps into the standard rectangular strip. Its upper-row labels are $a,b,c,d$ and its lower-row labels are $h,g,f,e$, both read from left to right; the corner trace across the strip is therefore $a,h,b,g,c,f,d,e$. Identify the strip boundary sides as prescribed by those same maps. Let $\alpha$ be the edge path across the strip from the left side of $a$ on the left boundary to the left side of $a$ on the right boundary, and let $\beta$ be the edge path on the left boundary from the base of $a$ to the top of $h$. Their ordered corner factors are respectively $z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1},z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1}$ and $z_2^{-1},w_1$. The face-pairing incidence check gives one positive transverse intersection, so their homology classes form a basis of $H_1$ and the loops form a basis of $\pi_1$ of the torus link. The two edge products are $z_1^2z_3w_1^2w_3$ and $z_2^2z_3w_2^2w_3$, while
$$H(\alpha)=\left(\frac{z_2z_3}{w_2w_3}\right)^2,\qquad H(\beta)=\frac{w_1}{z_2}.$$

A **covering map** is a continuous surjection $p:E\to B$ such that every $b\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets $V_j$, called **sheets**, and each restriction $p|_{V_j}:V_j\to U$ is a homeomorphism ([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]], [[def-disjoint-union-topology]]). Such a $U$ is **evenly covered**, and $p^{-1}(b)$ is the **fibre** over $b$. A covering is **trivial** when it is isomorphic over $B$ to a product projection $B\times F\to B$ with $F$ discrete.
For a covering $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$, the induced homomorphism $p_*:\pi_1(E,e_0)\to\pi_1(B,b_0)$ is injective.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for the chosen smooth knot-exterior data. Let $K_8$ be the standard figure-eight knot, presented as the boundary of the square plumbing of one positive and one negative Hopf band, with one boundary component. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose positive normal push-off of its core has linking number $+1$ with the core; a negative Hopf band has linking number $-1$. A square plumbing identifies a square in the boundary collars of the annuli with the four boundary edges alternating between the annuli, then smooths corners. With the twist convention that the positive twist $R_a$ sends $a\mapsto a$, $b\mapsto a+b$, and the negative twist $L_b$ sends $a\mapsto a+b$, $b\mapsto b$, the monodromy is $R_a\circ L_b$. Set $\rho(s)=1-s$ for $0\le s\le1$ and $\rho(s)=0$ for $1\le s\le2$. The map $J(c(x,s))=c(H_{\rho(s)}(x),s)$ on the collar, extended by the identity outside it, is a homeomorphism: its inverse replaces $H_{\rho(s)}$ with $H_{\rho(s)}^{-1}$. It restricts to $H_1$ at the boundary and is isotopic to the identity through the same formula with $H_{u\rho(s)}$ for $u\in[0,1]$. Thus $h_0=J|_{\partial V'}\circ h$ sends $\mu$ exactly to $\mu'$, and extending $h_0$ suffices because postcomposition with $J^{-1}$ recovers an extension of $h$ without changing its orientation sign.

Cut $V$ and $V'$ along the product meridian disks $D=D^2\times\{1\}$ and $D'=D^2\times\{1\}$. Each cut-open solid torus is $D^2\times[0,1]$. After centering the interval at $0$, this convex cylinder is homeomorphic to the unit ball by radial rescaling: in direction $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)\in S^2$ its boundary radius is $R(u)=\min\{(u_1^2+u_2^2)^{-1/2},(2|u_3|)^{-1}\}$, with a zero denominator interpreted as $+\infty$, and $(r,u)\mapsto rR(u)u$ gives the homeomorphism. The boundary of each cut-open torus consists of the annulus obtained by cutting the boundary torus along the meridian and two disk faces. The restriction of $h_0$ maps the annular portions to one another. Its common restriction to $\mu$ extends over each disk face by [F1], using the same disk map on both copies. The radial disk maps send the center of each disk face to the center of its target face. These maps assemble to a homeomorphism $\psi:\partial B\to\partial B'$ between the sphere boundaries of the cut-open balls, carrying the pair of disk-face centers to that pair in the target.

Identify each cut-open ball with the unit ball in $\mathbb R^3$. Apply [F1] with $d=3$ to extend $\psi$ radially over the ball. The cylinder-to-ball radial rescaling of step 2.1 carries the central product arc $\{0\}\times[0,1]$ to the diameter joining the two disk-face center points. Since $\psi$ carries those endpoints to the target pair, its radial extension carries this entire diameter to the corresponding target diameter. Thus the ball extension preserves the product core arc. The extension has orientation sign equal to the degree sign of $\psi$. On the open annulus away from the disk faces, $\psi$ is exactly $h_0$; cutting does not change the local boundary orientation there, so this degree sign is the orientation sign of $h_0$.

The two copies of each meridian disk receive the same disk map from [F1], so the ball extension agrees on their identified faces. It therefore descends after regluing to a homeomorphism $V\to V'$ extending $h_0$ and carrying the product core circle to the target core circle. Composing with $J^{-1}$ extends the original $h$; this collar-supported map fixes the core and keeps the same orientation sign because $J$ is isotopic to the identity.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

derivations.claim: Put $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$, $K=\mathrm{PSU}(2)$ and $V=\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$. Choose $X_1=\tfrac12\left(\begin{smallmatrix}i&0\\0&-i\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $X_2=\tfrac12\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $X_3=\tfrac12\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&i\\i&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ in $\mathfrak k$, and put $Y_j=iX_j$. These $Y_j$ are an orthonormal tangent basis for curvature $-1$ hyperbolic space; for example $\exp(tY_1)$ moves the basepoint distance $|t|$, and the $K$ action rotates this basis. The matrix commutators give $[X_i,X_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}X_k$ and $[Y_i,Y_j]=i\epsilon_{ijk}Y_k$. On $V$ let $R_j=\operatorname{ad}Y_j$. Each $Y_j$ is Hermitian, so $R_j$ is self-adjoint for $\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AB^*)$, by cyclicity of trace. The $K$ action is unitary for this product.

Represent $E$-valued forms by horizontal $K$-equivariant $V$-valued forms on $Q=\Gamma\backslash G$, expressing their coefficients in the left Maurer–Cartan frame. Indeed a frame $g$ identifies the fiber over $gK$ with $V$ by $\operatorname{Ad}g$, and replacing $g$ by $gk$ changes these coefficients by $\operatorname{Ad}k^{-1}$ and rotates the tangent indices. In these coefficients write $\varepsilon_j$ for exterior multiplication by the dual of $Y_j$ and $\iota_j$ for contraction by $Y_j$. The ordinary covariant differential of the $K$ connection is $D=\sum_j\varepsilon_jY_j$, because the horizontal part of $[Y_i,Y_j]$ is zero. Differentiating the fiber change $\operatorname{Ad}g$ gives $d_E=D+T$, where $T=\sum_j\varepsilon_jR_j$. These are actual coefficient formulas on all degrees, not definitions of a different connection.

The invariant volume on $Q$ is the product of hyperbolic volume and normalized compact-fiber volume. Integration in a local bundle chart and then a subordinate smooth partition of unity [F2] shows that integration of a $K$-invariant coefficient norm on $Q$ equals its integration on $M$. The left invariant fields $Y_j$ have zero divergence for this volume: $G$ is unimodular, since $\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}Z)=0$ for the displayed Lie algebra basis, hence for all $Z$, and $\det\operatorname{Ad}(\exp Z)=1$. Right translation therefore preserves its Haar volume. Integration by parts on compact supports now gives $D^*=-\sum_j\iota_jY_j$ and $T^*=\sum_j\iota_jR_j$. The relations $\varepsilon_i\iota_j+\iota_j\varepsilon_i=\delta_{ij}$ show that $DT^*+T^*D+TD^*+D^*T=0$: the two anticommutator sums are respectively $\sum_jR_jY_j$ and its negative, since coefficient differentiation commutes with the constant matrices $R_j$. Thus $d_E\delta_E+\delta_Ed_E=DD^*+D^*D+H$, where $H=TT^*+T^*T$. All statements are $K$-equivariant and descend from $Q$ to $M$.

On one-form coefficients $a=(a_1,a_2,a_3)\in V^3$, the exterior-contraction relations give $(Ha)_i=\sum_jR_j^2a_i+\sum_j[R_i,R_j]a_j$. This finite-dimensional self-adjoint operator is positive definite. If $Ha=0$, positivity of $TT^*+T^*T$ gives $Ta=0$, namely $R_ia_j=R_ja_i$ for all $i,j$. Since $[R_i,R_j]=i\epsilon_{ijk}R_k$, the commutator sum in the displayed formula is a multiple of $R_ka_j-R_ja_k$ and vanishes. Consequently $0=\langle Ha,a\rangle=\sum_{i,j}\|R_ja_i\|^2$. Each $a_i$ commutes with all $Y_j$, which span $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ over $\mathbb C$. A matrix commuting with all traceless matrices is scalar, and a traceless scalar is zero. Thus $a=0$. Compactness of the unit sphere in $V^3$ supplies $c>0$ with $H\ge cI$.

For a compactly supported smooth one-form, integration by parts in step 3.1 and step 4.1 give $\|d_E\alpha\|_2^2+\|\delta_E\alpha\|_2^2=\|D\alpha\|_2^2+\|D^*\alpha\|_2^2+(H\alpha,\alpha)\ge c\|\alpha\|_2^2$. We next extend this inequality to the joint weak graph domain. On each cusp choose a smooth cutoff equal to one for $t\le R$, zero for $t\ge2R$, with derivative bounded by $C/R$, and set it equal to one on the compact core. These cutoffs $\chi_R$ have compact support and $|d\chi_R|\le C/R$. For a weak graph-domain form $v$, the product formulas $d_E(\chi_Rv)=\chi_Rd_Ev+d\chi_R\wedge v$ and $\delta_E(\chi_Rv)=\chi_R\delta_Ev-\iota_{\nabla\chi_R}v$ show convergence to $v$ in the joint graph norm. The same conclusion holds separately for each differential and codifferential and for forms of every degree. In the compact case take the cutoff identically one.

Here are the local smoothing details needed to finish that graph-density argument. In a finite collection of trivializing charts around the support of $\chi_Rv$, every differential or codifferential is a first-order matrix operator $P=\sum_jA_j(x)\partial_j+B(x)$ with smooth coefficients. Multiplication by a subordinate smooth partition [F2] reduces to forms supported inside individual charts. For convolution with a smooth unit-mass kernel $\rho_\epsilon$, the difference $P(v*\rho_\epsilon)-(Pv)*\rho_\epsilon$ is a sum of integral operators with kernels $(A_j(x)-A_j(y))\partial_j\rho_\epsilon(x-y)+(\partial_jA_j)(y)\rho_\epsilon(x-y)$ and a zero-order coefficient commutator. The $L^1$ kernel bounds are uniform on the compact chart, by the mean-value bound for $A_j$ and scaling of $\rho_\epsilon$; thus these commutators are uniformly bounded on $L^2$. They tend to zero on smooth functions by differentiation of convolutions, hence on all $L^2$ functions by the smooth-density fact in [F2] and the uniform bound. Therefore local mollification converges in each asserted graph norm, also for the direct sum operator $(d_E,\delta_E)$. The partition contributes only fixed zero-order commutators, so a finite sum completes the approximation by compactly supported smooth forms. Together with step 5.1 this proves the coercive inequality on the maximal joint graph domain. It also proves that maximal differentials are the adjoints of maximal formal codifferentials, since their compact-support integration-by-parts identities extend by this graph density.

Let $\mathcal H_p=L^2(\Lambda^pT^*M\otimes E)$ and let $d_p$ be the maximal weak differential. It is closed: convergence of a form and its differential in $L^2$ preserves the weak test-function identity. Flatness gives $d_1d_0=0$ distributionally. Put $Z=\ker d_1$, a closed subspace of $\mathcal H_1$, and $\delta=d_0^*$. Every $w\in Z^\perp$ belongs to $\operatorname{Dom}\delta$ with $\delta w=0$, because it is orthogonal to $\operatorname{ran}d_0\subseteq Z$. Hence the orthogonal projection $P_Z$ maps $\operatorname{Dom}\delta$ into itself and $\delta P_Zv=\delta v$. On $Z\cap\operatorname{Dom}\delta$, steps 5.1 and 6.1 give $\|v\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\delta v\|_2$. In particular $A=\delta|_{Z\cap\operatorname{Dom}\delta}$ is injective with closed range: a Cauchy sequence of its images is, by this estimate, the image under the closed operator $\delta$ of a convergent sequence in $Z$.

Fix a weakly closed $\alpha\in\mathcal H_1$, so $\alpha\in Z$. On the closed range of $A$ define $\ell(Av)=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$. It is well defined and bounded, with norm at most $c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$, by step 7.1. Extend it to $\mathcal H_0$ by zero on the orthogonal complement of that range and use [F1] to obtain $b\in\mathcal H_0$ with $\langle Av,b\rangle=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$ and $\|b\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$. For arbitrary $v\in\operatorname{Dom}\delta$, replace $v$ by $P_Zv$; its $\delta$ image is unchanged and its pairing with $\alpha$ is unchanged. Thus $\langle\delta v,b\rangle=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$ on the full domain of $\delta$. By the adjoint definition and the graph-density conclusion of step 6.1, $b\in\operatorname{Dom}d_0$ and $d_0b=\alpha$. This proves the primitive assertion in the weak sense without an external closed-range or harmonic-representative theorem.

If $\alpha$ is smooth, the primitive $b$ is smooth. In a flat parallel frame on a coordinate ball, $d_Eb=\alpha$ is the ordinary componentwise distributional equation $db=\alpha$. A smooth closed one-form on a smaller star-shaped coordinate ball has a smooth primitive $b_0$, given by integrating along straight radial segments; differentiating the integral and using closedness verifies $db_0=\alpha$. Then $d(b-b_0)=0$ distributionally. Mollification on still smaller balls makes this difference a sequence of constants, so its distributional limit is constant as well. Thus $b=b_0+\text{constant}$ is smooth locally and hence globally. Its $L^2$ norm and the bound from step 8.1 remain unchanged.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every compact smooth manifold, with boundary

supplied finite CW manifold, the collar may be retained in a finite relative CW
model.

For $A\subseteq X$ and a local system $\mathcal L$ on $X$, restriction to $A$ gives natural exact sequences
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\partial}H_{n-1}(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to\cdots$$

The homology connector sends a relative cycle represented by $c$ to $[\partial c]$. The cohomology connector sends a cocycle $a$ on $A$ to $[\delta\widetilde a]$, where $\widetilde a$ is its extension by zero to simplices not contained in $A$. Naturality uses the variances of the preceding functoriality proposition.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $n$-manifold and let $A=\partial M$; let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and $\mathcal L$ an $R$-module local system on $M$. Cap with the canonical relative twisted fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $k$,
$$H^k(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M,A;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L),\qquad H^k(M,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L).$$
Here $\mathcal O_M^R$ is the collar extension of the interior orientation system. The statement is for the actual boundary $A$, not an arbitrary subspace of $M$.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let
$f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$.
Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible:

$$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$

Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique
holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that

$$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$

and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed,

$$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Let $Z$ be a reduced complex analytic space with point $o$, and suppose $u_i,v_i,a_i,b_i$ are holomorphic germs on $Z$ for $1\le i\le k$, with $k<\infty$, $u_i(o)=v_i(o)=0$, $a_i(o)\ne0$ and $\tau_i^0=b_i(o)/a_i(o)\notin\mathbb R$. Suppose the affine maps
$$L_i(w)=e^{u_i}w+a_i,\qquad P_i(w)=e^{v_i}w+b_i$$
commute at every parameter point. Then, after shrinking around $o$, there are holomorphic germs $\tau_i$ such that $v_i=\tau_i u_i$, $\tau_i(o)=\tau_i^0$ and $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i\ne0$ throughout. In particular $u_i=0$ if and only if $v_i=0$, and $v_i/u_i\to\tau_i^0$ as the parameter tends to $o$ through $u_i\ne0$. No smoothness, dimension or rank hypothesis on $Z$ is required.

For $u_i\ne0$, there is a unique real pair $(p_i,q_i)$ solving $p_iu_i+q_iv_i=2\pi i$. With
$$\widetilde u_i=\frac{2\pi i}{p_i+\tau_i^0q_i},$$
one has
$$|\widetilde u_i-u_i|\le\frac{|\tau_i-\tau_i^0|}{|\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0|}|u_i|.$$
Set $\widetilde u_i=0$ when $u_i=0$. The functions $\widetilde u_i$ are continuous at such points, and $\|\widetilde u-u\|=o(\|u\|)$ as the parameter tends to $o$ through $u\ne0$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a boundaryless Riemannian manifold. An open set $W\subseteq M$ is called **strongly geodesically convex** here when, for every ordered pair $(x,y)\in W\times W$, there is a unique affinely parametrized geodesic $\gamma_{x,y}:[0,1]\to M$ that globally minimizes length from $x$ to $y$, its image lies in $W$, and $(x,y,t)\mapsto\gamma_{x,y}(t)$ is smooth.

Every point of $M$ has a strongly geodesically convex neighbourhood. More precisely, the neighbourhood may be chosen inside any prescribed open neighbourhood of the point, and it may be chosen so that every piecewise smooth curve attaining the global minimum between two of its points is a monotone reparametrization of the displayed connector. Every nonempty intersection of a positive finite family of strongly geodesically convex open sets is again strongly geodesically convex.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Every open cover of a smooth manifold has a countable cover by coordinate balls with compact closures, each closure contained in one member of the original cover.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(U_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a countable cover of a smooth manifold $M$ by coordinate balls with compact closures. Then there is an at-most-countable index set $I$ and families of open sets $(W_k)_{k\in I}$ and coordinate balls $(V_k)_{k\in I}$ such that $M=\bigcup_{k\in I} W_k$, each $\overline{W_k}\subseteq V_k\subseteq \overline{V_k}\subseteq U_{n(k)}$ for some index $n(k)$, and the family $(V_k)$ is locally finite. The index set may be finite or empty.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

derivations.claim: The complete holonomy is irreducible and its adjoint invariants vanish. Indeed one cusp subgroup is a rank-two translation lattice fixing $\infty$. If all of $\Gamma$ fixed $\infty$, its elements would be similarities $z\mapsto az+b$. An element with $|a|\ne1$ would conjugate a fixed nonzero lattice translation to translations tending to the identity, contradicting discreteness. An element with $|a|=1$ and $a\ne1$ is elliptic about a vertical line, impossible in a torsion-free discrete group. Hence all elements would be translations, and the quotient would have infinite volume as height tends to zero. This contradicts the finite-volume hypothesis. Thus some element does not fix $\infty$. A traceless matrix invariant under the cusp group is a multiple of $E=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, by direct commutation with a nontrivial unipotent. A nonzero such matrix invariant under all of $\Gamma$ would force preservation of its kernel line, hence of $\infty$, a contradiction. Thus $H^0(M;E_{\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0})=0$. The same argument excludes a common invariant line for the holonomy matrices. The group centralizer in $G$ is trivial as well: a Möbius map commuting with the cusp translations fixes $\infty$ and is itself a translation, by its affine formula; a nonidentity such translation has unique fixed point $\infty$, so commuting with the entire group would force the whole group to fix $\infty$.

We specify the cohomology comparisons being used. The flat adjoint bundle has local parallel frames, obtained on simply connected balls by trivializing its defining covering construction. In such frames its differential is the componentwise ordinary exterior differential; integration of forms over simplices is compatible with the constant transition matrices and with Stokes. The usual local Poincaré contraction is explicit: integrate contraction by the radial vector along radial coordinate segments. A locally finite good cover by sufficiently small strongly convex metric balls therefore gives a Čech double complex whose form columns resolve the parallel local sections. Its positive Čech rows are contracted by $(hc)_{i_0\ldots i_{r-1}}=\sum_j\phi_jc_{ji_0\ldots i_{r-1}}$, for a subordinate partition of unity. The small-singular-cochain double complex has the same degree-zero columns, since every intersection is contractible; subdivision makes singular simplices subordinate to the cover, and the Čech rows contract by assigning a containing index to each small simplex. The two edge comparisons identify flat de Rham cohomology with singular cohomology with this local system, naturally for restrictions. These constructions also apply to compact support and to collars, so relative classes are represented by forms supported away from the ends. Finally $M$ is aspherical, with universal cover $\mathbb H^3$ contractible. Its lifted cellular or singular chains form a free resolution of $\mathbb C$ as a $\mathbb C\Gamma$-module; comparison of free resolutions by successive lifts gives the same cohomology as group cocycles. In degree one, this comparison is concretely integration of an equivariant closed form along a lifted group loop. These arguments establish the coefficient comparisons, rather than invoking an unproved twisted de Rham theorem.

The representation scheme of a torus is smooth near its noncentral complete peripheral pair. Use local $SL_2$ lifts $A,B$ of the two generators, both near nontrivial commuting unipotents; their commutator is $I$ because its sign is locally constant and is positive at the basepoint. Choose a fixed vector $v$ with $v,Av$ independent at that point and hence nearby. For a commuting matrix $B$, write $Bv=av+bAv$; commutation then forces $B=aI+bA$ by applying both sides to the basis $v,Av$. This argument works over truncated power-series rings too, because the basis determinant is a unit. Put $C=A-(\operatorname{tr}A)I/2$ and write $B=\alpha I+\beta C$. Its determinant condition is $\alpha^2-\beta^2((\operatorname{tr}A)^2/4-1)=1$. At the complete pair $\alpha=1$, so [F3] solves uniquely for $\alpha$ in terms of $A$ and $\beta$. Thus the commuting-pair scheme is locally a smooth four-dimensional space, parametrized by the three coordinates of $A$ and one of $\beta$. In particular every representation over $\mathbb C[t]/(t^{n+1})$ near this pair extends one order further.

Write $E_0=E_{\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0}$. The restriction $r_1:H^1(N;E_0)\to H^1(\partial N;E_0)$ is injective. If a closed smooth form represents a class in its kernel, on each cusp tail it equals $d_{E_0}b_i$ for a smooth section, by step 1.2. Subtract $d_{E_0}(\chi_i b_i)$ using a cutoff equal to one sufficiently far along that end and zero near the core. The resulting cohomologous closed form is compactly supported, hence square integrable, and is exact by [F1]. Thus the original class is zero. Equivalently the map $H^1(N,\partial N;E_0)\to H^1(N;E_0)$ vanishes. By [F2], its transpose, up to the harmless cap-boundary sign, is the map $H^2(N,\partial N;E_0)\to H^2(N;E_0)$, so that map also vanishes. The pair sequence therefore gives $r_2:H^2(N;E_0)\to H^2(\partial N;E_0)$ injective. It is onto because its cokernel embeds in $H^3(N,\partial N;E_0)$, which is dual to $H^0(N;E_0)=0$ by step 1.1.

We give the full obstruction construction. Suppose $\rho^{(n)}$ is a representation over $\mathbb C[t]/(t^{n+1})$ with constant term $\rho_0$. Choose arbitrary one-order lifts $\widetilde\rho(\gamma)$ of its values. The defect is uniquely $\widetilde\rho(\gamma)\widetilde\rho(\delta)\widetilde\rho(\gamma\delta)^{-1}=I+t^{n+1}c(\gamma,\delta)$ modulo $t^{n+2}$, with $c$ in the adjoint Lie algebra; this expression is read in the identity chart of $G$. Associativity gives $c(\gamma,\delta)+c(\gamma\delta,\epsilon)=\operatorname{Ad}_{\rho_0(\gamma)}c(\delta,\epsilon)+c(\gamma,\delta\epsilon)$, exactly the group two-cocycle relation. Replacing the lift at $\gamma$ by $(I+t^{n+1}b(\gamma))\widetilde\rho(\gamma)$ changes $c$ by $b(\gamma)+\operatorname{Ad}_{\rho_0(\gamma)}b(\delta)-b(\gamma\delta)$. Hence a one-order extension exists if and only if the class $[c]\in H^2(\Gamma;\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0)$ vanishes. The formulas commute with restriction to every subgroup.

At a cusp the adjoint invariants are $\mathbb CE$, of dimension one. Torus duality and the Euler characteristic of a finite cellular local system give $\dim H^0(T_i;E_0)=\dim H^2(T_i;E_0)=1$ and $\dim H^1(T_i;E_0)=2$. Indeed every cell contributes three coefficient dimensions, so the alternating chain dimension is $3\chi(T_i)=0$. The pair sequence and step 2.1 give a short exact sequence $0\to H^1(N;E_0)\to H^1(\partial N;E_0)\to H^2(N,\partial N;E_0)\to0$. The last group is dual to the first by [F2]. Consequently $\dim H^1(N;E_0)=k$, while $r_2$ identifies $H^2(N;E_0)$ with $\mathbb C^k$. All these spaces are finite dimensional by the finite CW model in [F2].

On each peripheral subgroup the obstruction in step 2.2 is zero by the smooth formal chart of step 1.3. The map on $H^2$ restricting to all peripheral subgroups is injective by step 2.1 and the comparisons in step 1.2, so the global obstruction vanishes. Starting with any first-order cocycle, repeat step 2.2 and choose corrections at each order. AC supplies this countable recursive sequence. Every first-order representation tangent vector therefore has a full formal representation curve with that tangent. No convergence assertion about this curve is needed.

We compute the cusp classes and trace derivatives. Normalize the cusp lattice as $z=x+\tau_i^0 y$, with deck translations $x\mapsto x+1$ and $y\mapsto y+1$, and put $F=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ and $n(z)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&z\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The forms $\eta_i=dx\otimes E$ and $\omega_i=dz\otimes\operatorname{Ad}_{n(z)}F$ are equivariant and closed: $E$ is translation invariant and the polynomial $\operatorname{Ad}_{n(z)}F=F+zH-z^2E$ depends only on $z$, so its derivative wedges to zero with $dz$. Their trace-paired cup product is $\operatorname{tr}(\eta_i\wedge\omega_i)=\tau_i^0dx\wedge dy$, while each self-pairing is zero. Thus these two classes are independent and form a basis by step 3.1. The form $\eta_i$ is square integrable on its cusp: at height $t$, $|dx|$ grows as $e^t$ and the homogeneous norm of $E$ decays as $e^{-t}$, whereas volume decays as $e^{-2t}$.

Let $L$ be the span of the $k$ classes $\eta_i$ in $H^1(\partial N;E_0)$. The image of $r_1$ meets $L$ only in zero. If a global closed form restricts cohomologically to a combination of these $\eta_i$, subtract exact cutoff terms on the ends as in step 2.1 to arrange equality with that combination on each tail. The resulting global form is square integrable by step 4.1 and compactness of the remaining core, hence exact by [F1]. Since both $H^1(N;E_0)$ and the span of the $\omega_i$ have dimension $k$, there is a global cohomology basis whose boundary images are $\omega_i+\sum_jc_{ij}\eta_j$.

A group one-cocycle $a$ represents the infinitesimal representation $(I+\epsilon a(\gamma))\rho_0(\gamma)$ modulo $\epsilon^2$, as direct multiplication verifies; infinitesimal conjugacies are precisely coboundaries. Thus representation tangent vectors modulo infinitesimal conjugacy are $H^1(N;E_0)$. For the positive local lift of the normalized cusp meridian, $\rho_0(\mu_i)=n(1)$, integration in step 1.2 gives $a_{\eta_i}(\mu_i)=E$ and $a_{\omega_i}(\mu_i)=\int_0^1(F+xH-x^2E)\,dx=F+H/2-E/3$. Therefore $d\operatorname{tr}_{\mu_i}(\eta_i)=\operatorname{tr}(En(1))=0$ and $d\operatorname{tr}_{\mu_i}(\omega_i)=1$. For trace squared the latter derivative is $4$, since the complete trace is $2$. Classes supported at other cusps contribute only their own restrictions. By the basis in step 5.1, $(ds_1,\ldots,ds_k)$ is an isomorphism from $H^1(N;E_0)$ to $\mathbb C^k$. This is a tangent calculation; smoothness is proved next.

Here is why formal integrability implies analytic smoothness in this setting, without an approximation theorem for formal solutions. Take a finite presentation from [F2] and express its relators near $\rho_0$ as an analytic map $R:\mathbb C^{3g}\to\mathbb C^{3r}$ by using local coordinates on $G$ for the generators and the identity logarithm for each relator. Put $K_0=\ker dR_0$, choose a complement $W$ in the source and a projection $\pi$ onto $\operatorname{im}dR_0$ in the target. By [F3], the equation $\pi R(z,w)=0$ has the unique solution $w=\psi(z)$, with $z\in K_0$, $\psi(0)=0$ and $d\psi_0=0$. Thus the representation germ is the zero set of $\kappa(z)=(I-\pi)R(z,\psi(z))$. If $\kappa$ were nonzero, let $P_d$ be its first nonzero homogeneous Taylor term. A formal representation curve of arbitrary tangent $a\in K_0$, supplied by step 3.2, has $z(t)=ta+O(t^2)$ and $w(t)=\psi(z(t))$; the latter identity follows recursively from the invertible partial Jacobian defining $\psi$. Its relators then give $P_d(a)=0$. This holds for every $a\in K_0$, contradicting that $P_d$ is a nonzero polynomial. Hence $\kappa$ vanishes identically by convergence of its analytic Taylor series. The representation scheme is smooth with tangent $K_0=Z^1(\Gamma;\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0)$ and dimension $k+3$: $H^1$ has dimension $k$, and the coboundaries have dimension three because the invariants vanish in step 1.1.

To pass to ordinary conjugacy, choose three linear coordinate conditions transverse to the conjugation orbit at $\rho_0$. The orbit derivative is injective by step 1.1. The analytic inverse theorem, equivalently [F3] applied to the conjugation map, gives a local product of a three-dimensional identity neighborhood in $G$ and a slice $S$ of dimension $k$. This slice represents the actual conjugacy quotient germ. To exclude extra identifications by large conjugations, suppose instead that arbitrarily near $\rho_0$ there were conjugate pairs requiring conjugators away from the identity in $G$. Choose such a sequence, lift its conjugators to nonzero matrices and normalize their Euclidean matrix norms to one. After a subsequence the normalized matrices have a nonzero limit $P$. Choose local lifts of the finitely many generator matrices. Their intertwining equations have signs $\pm1$; after another subsequence each sign is fixed. If $P$ had rank one, these equations would make its kernel a common invariant line of the limiting holonomy matrices, contradicting step 1.1. Thus $P$ is invertible, and its projective class centralizes the complete holonomy. That projective centralizer is trivial by step 1.1, so the conjugators tend projectively to the identity, a contradiction. The local product uniqueness therefore excludes all extra slice identifications after shrinking. This proves smoothness of the ordinary quotient germ. By step 6.1 the trace-squared map on $S$ has invertible differential, and [F3] makes $(s_1,\ldots,s_k)$ its holomorphic coordinates.

Let $u\in\mathbb C^k$ be small. Step 8.1 gives a unique slice representation $\rho(u)$ whose trace-squared coordinates are $s_i=4\cosh^2(u_i/2)$; it depends holomorphically on $u$. Choose local $SL_2$ lifts $A_i(u)$ of $\rho(u)(\mu_i)$ with trace near $2$. Their traces equal $2\cosh(u_i/2)$, because their squares agree and the near-$2$ branch is unique. Thus $e^{u_i/2}$ is an eigenvalue. The matrix $A_i(u)-e^{u_i/2}I$ has rank one throughout a small neighborhood, including $u_i=0$, since it has zero determinant and stays near a nonzero rank-one matrix. A fixed nonzero column of its adjugate gives a holomorphic kernel line $\ell_i(u)$ after shrinking. This line is invariant under the whole peripheral subgroup by commutation. Conversely, given a nearby slice representation with a chosen peripheral line, its meridian eigenvalue on that line is holomorphic and near $1$; its unique near-zero ratio logarithm defines $u_i$. The trace relation forces precisely the representation just constructed, and the rank-one kernel forces precisely its chosen line. Both constructions are holomorphic: the eigenvalue is read by applying the matrix to a local nonzero vector of the line. They are inverse maps on the augmented germ. Hence that germ is smooth of dimension $k$ with coordinates $u$.

The local lift of $\rho(u)(\lambda_i)$ commutes with $A_i(u)$: the commutator sign is locally constant and positive at the complete point. It acts on $\ell_i(u)$ by a nonzero holomorphic eigenvalue near its complete value; choose its sign to make this value $1$, and define $v_i$ as twice its near-zero logarithm. Choose a holomorphic change of frame sending $\ell_i(u)$ to $\mathbb Ce_1$, by adjoining a fixed complementary vector and normalizing the determinant locally. The resulting peripheral Möbius maps fix $\infty$ and act on its finite complement as $z\mapsto e^{u_i}z+a_i(u)$ and $z\mapsto e^{v_i}z+b_i(u)$. At $u=0$, their translations satisfy $a_i(0)\ne0$ and $b_i(0)/a_i(0)=\tau_i^0$. Apply [F4] to get $v_i=\tau_i(u)u_i$ with $\tau_i$ holomorphic and $\tau_i(0)=\tau_i^0$. Positivity of the imaginary part persists on a sufficiently small common neighborhood. For one cusp the holomorphic Taylor expansion gives $v(u)=\tau^0u+O(u^2)$. All constructions used representation matrices and cusp models; none used an ideal triangulation, or a positivity assumption about tetrahedra.
